sentences.t: In the spring of fourteen fifty three, the city of Constantinople was a shadow of what it had been.
Its population had fallen to maybe fifty thousand people, rattling around inside walls built for half a million.
The empire that called itself Roman was, by now, really just this one city and a few scraps of land in Greece.
And camped outside those walls was the Ottoman sultan Mehmed the Second, twenty one years old, with an army of perhaps eighty thousand men.
Now, those walls were the most famous fortifications in the medieval world.
They had held for a thousand years against Avars, Persians, Arabs, Bulgars, and everyone else who'd tried.
But Mehmed had something none of them had.
He had guns, and very, very large ones.

So, the guns.
A Hungarian engineer called Orban had first offered his services to the Byzantine emperor, Constantine the Eleventh.
Constantine couldn't afford him.
So Orban walked across the lines and offered them to Mehmed instead, who could.
The result was a bronze cannon over eight meters long that fired stone balls weighing more than half a ton.
It took sixty oxen to drag it into position, and it could only fire about seven times a day.
But every shot that hit took a bite out of walls that had never been designed for this.
The defenders did something remarkable, though.
Every night they rebuilt the damage with timber, earth, rubble, and barrels packed with dirt.
And for weeks, every morning, the Ottomans found the wall they'd broken the day before standing again.
There was a second problem for Mehmed, and that was the water.
The Byzantines had stretched an enormous chain across the mouth of the Golden Horn, the harbor on the city's northern side.
His fleet simply couldn't get in.
So, in one of the strangest moves in military history, he went around it.
His men built a road of greased logs over the hill behind Galata and dragged around seventy ships overland, down into the harbor.
Imagine standing on the sea wall one morning and watching warships come sliding down a hillside toward you.
Now the defenders had to man a whole new stretch of wall they'd thought was safe, with men they didn't have.
The final assault came before dawn on the twenty ninth of May.
Wave after wave, first irregulars, then regular troops, and finally the Janissaries, the sultan's elite.
Somewhere in the chaos, a small gate called the Kerkoporta was apparently left open.
Whether that story is true or not, the Ottoman flag was soon flying on the walls.
Constantine the Eleventh, the last Roman emperor, threw off his imperial regalia and charged into the fighting.
His body was never identified with certainty.
In the next part, we'll look at what Mehmed did with the city, and why he started calling himself Caesar of Rome.
Thanks for watching, and I'll see you then.
